props.title: Kill Rommel!
props.initialSlug: One man's mission to end Rommel

sections.content: This obscure 1969 World War II action film directed by Henry Hathaway represents a unique entry in the North African campaign subgenre. While more famous films like The Desert Fox (1951) and **Patton** (1970) portrayed Field Marshal Erwin Rommel as a complex, even sympathetic figure, **Kill Rommel! (1969)** (1969) takes a straightforward commando mission approach. The film follows a British Special Air Service (SAS) team attempting to assassinate the legendary German commander, drawing inspiration from actual failed Allied attempts to target Rommel during the desert war.

sections.content: The North African theater spawned numerous films focusing on special operations and raids, with Tobruk (1967) and Raid on Rommel (1971) following similar narrative patterns of Allied forces attempting decisive strikes behind enemy lines. These films helped establish many conventions of the desert warfare subgenre - the harsh environment as an enemy itself, the cat-and-mouse tactical games, and the grudging respect between opposing commanders.

While **Kill Rommel!** (1969) may lack the production values of later WWII epics like **The Desert Rats** (1953) or **The English Patient** (1996), it captures the gritty determination of early SAS operations. The film's straightforward mission structure influenced later special operations war films like **The Wild Geese** (1978) and **Who Dares Wins** (1982). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Rommel on Film

sections.content: The cinematic portrayal of Erwin Rommel evolved significantly from post-war admiration to more nuanced examination. The Desert Fox (1951) and **The Desert Rats** (1953) presented him as an honorable warrior, while later films like **Patton** (1970) and **Valkyrie** (2008) explored his eventual disillusionment with Hitler's regime. **Kill Rommel!** (1969) stands as an interesting transitional piece, treating him more as a pure military target than a complex historical figure.
